speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Will the minister investigate a report that construction companies engaged on federal work at La Scie, Newfoundland, are working men 60 hours per week with no overtime rates except for hours in excess of 60 hours per week, and that local men are being paid less than men from the mainland for the same work; and will the minister take steps to ensure that proper employment practices are followed ir this area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: OVERTIME AND WAGE RATES ON FEDERAL WORKS AT LA SCIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was kind enough to send me notice of his question. Two contractors are engaged at La Scie, Newfoundland. Gulf Maritime Construction Limited is working on a harbour development project under a contract with the Department of Public Works. This is part of a federal-provincial joint project for the improvement of the harbour and the construction of a fish plant. Terminal Construction Company Limited is working on a project for the United States army corps of engineers.
Wage rates and hours of labour for workers employed on both contracts are governed by the federal Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act. The statutory hours of labour under this act are 8 per day and 44 per week. These statutory hours can be extended by the Minister of Labour in emergency circumstances.
On the urgent representations of the parties concerned that emergency conditions existed justifying an extension of the hours worked, both contractors were given authority to extend hours to a maximum of 10 per day and 60 per week. The overtime authority issued to these contractors included the following conditions:
(a)	That no employee be required to work in excess of such maximum hours;
(b)	that penalty overtime rates may be invoked in connection with the provisions of section 2 of the labour conditions forming part of the contract;
(c)	that payroll records be maintained
showing all hours worked by each employee in excess of the statutory hours, and

I should like to point out to hon. members that this follows the same wording, with only one minor necessary change, contained in section 111 of the Unemployment Insurance

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR NEW THREE-YEAR POOL, MAXIMUM GUARANTEE OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister has told us that there is a similar provision in the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am rather surprised that provision is there but, of course, there is a great deal of difference between the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act and an act to provide for loans to farmers. There may or may not be justification for that section in the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do suggest, as was urged on May 1 when this was last before us, that there is no justification for this section in the present bill. The amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Kamloops should commend itself to the committee and also, I would say, especially to the house leader and to all hon. members.
I can tell the minister, for instance, that we have a similar act to this which was passed last year, namely the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act, and it does not contain any such provision. Yet the situation is parallel, or certainly analogous. In one case loans are made to fishermen, and in the other to farmers. The department and this house did not see fit to include such a provision last year. We have the Canadian Farm Loan Act, which I have gone over rather carefully. There is no provision similar to this or in any way comparable to it in the Canadian Farm Loan Act, although there the loan may run for a period of 25 years, as the minister knows; yet such a provision is not contained therein.
I presume the minister's research staff has given considerable attention to this, and apparently the only matter the minister has been able to turn up which is comparable in wording at least

though I do not think it is comparable as far as the principle of the legislation is concerned-is the provision in the Unemployment Insurance Act, which I have not had an opportunity to read since he mentioned it. I presume in that case if a man has made false statements and misled
Farm Improvement Loans Act the unemployment insurance commission and thus obtained unemployment insurance when he should not have obtained it, there might be some possible reason for such a provision.
Just to recapitulate for a moment, and without unduly taking the time of the committee, I want to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that we are considering clause 5 of the bill which re-enacts section 8 of the original act. I shall read the clause which is being reenacted:
Any person who makes a statement in an application for a guaranteed farm improvement loan that is false in any material respect or who uses the proceeds of such loan for a purpose other than that stated in his application, is guilty of an offence-
These are the critical words to which I would draw the attention of the committee. -and liable on summary conviction to a fine of not more than $500.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, as you very well appreciate and as those of us who are lawyers appreciate, this invokes the provisions of the summary convictions act, the federal act which is a part of our Criminal Code and therefore we would have the time limits of that act invoked were it not for the succeeding section which goes on to say:
Proceedings for an offence under this section may be commenced at any time-
I repeat:
-at any time, within 12 months from the day on which evidence, sufficient in the opinion of the minister to justify prosecution for the offence, comes to his knowledge.
That is the particular point to which I wanted to draw the attention of the committee. As was said the other night, subsection 4 provides for a certificate signed by the minister or by someone authorized by the minister. I think that is going rather far afield, but at the moment I am not quarrelling with that wording. I do realize it is standard practice today, and it is obviously a wise practice. Instead of bringing witnesses before a court and proving certain things you can simply accept the signature. As far as I am concerned I would not quarrel with the signature of the minister or someone authorized on his behalf. What I am quarrelling with and suggesting is wrong and improper is the provision in this bill which permits the prosecution to be brought on at any indefinite time in the future provided it is within 12 months after it has been brought to the minister's attention.
As the hon. member for Kamloops pointed out the other night, and I think I did as well, the Criminal Code has a period of limitation. There are various offences under the summary convictions act, and most of those can be prosecuted only within a period

Farm Improvement Loans Act ol six months after the commission of the offence. As the hon. member for Kamloops pointed out even in treason, which is a capital offence-or was under the old code and I suspect it still is although I have not checked it; in any case it is one of the most serious offences with which a man can be charged-the information must be laid and the prosecution instituted within three years from the date of the commission of the offence. Here you have a section which says a man may be prosecuted within 12 months after it has come to the attention of the minister and it may not come to the minister's attention until 10 or 15 years after the alleged offence has been committed. The minister said it would not be advisable to have this extended, but I do not accept that for a moment.
I would point out that as I see it there is nothing in this section which ties in with the time limit even after the expiration of the loan. In other words a farmer may have repaid a loan, we will say within eighteen months, and then forgotten about it; yet under this bill it would be theoretically possible to bring a prosecution eight years afterwards. I am not saying, and the minister knows this very well, that a responsible minister of this government is likely to do such a thing. We realize that practical common sense will probably be applied to the application of this legislation, but I am asking if that is a satisfactory answer to this committee.
We are establishing a precedent here. I admit that there may have possibly been an unfortunate precedent established in connection with the Unemployment Insurance Act, but if so two wrongs do not make a right. The mere fact that we happened to have made a mistake, if we did make one, is no reason why we should make another.
The Minister of Finance, the house leader, has been a practising lawyer. He has been brought up in the school of our law and has carried on a country practice. He knows the general background of this whole problem. I suggest to him as a man with that background and with that training-I know he cannot answer personally, but I am putting it to him that he knows the answer-that a provision such as this is not in keeping with our concept of the law and would establish a most unfortunate precedent. If we have a period of limitation for the most serious offences which are prescribed by our law, then I suggest that certainly there should be one for this.
One could speak on this indefinitely, but I do not propose to do so. I am not trying to delay the committee, but I do submit that
	-	!
the amendment which is before this committee is one which should commend itself to all hon. members. It is not striking anything pertinent out of the bill, it is simply striking out this provision. 1 would even be willing to have the amendment amended by having some provision inserted whereby a report in writing could be made rather than actual evidence being submitted. It would be acceptable to me to have a document signed by the minister, or by someone authorized to sign on his behalf, taken as evidence. I would go that far, but I am completely opposed, and I trust this committee is opposed, to a provision being inserted in this particular legislation dealing with farmers, who I think are as honest as most classes in our community, whereby they shall be put in a special category.
It would be theoretically-I emphasize that -possible for an agent of the Department of Finance or the Department of Justice to institute proceedings against a man when he had forgotten completely the particulars of the transaction. I say that is wrong. Just a few days ago we had before this house a bill to amend the Income Tax Act to cut down still further the period allowed under that act. There the Department of Finance has fixed a period of six years except in cases where fraud can be established. Why should we depart from all accepted principles on this occasion, particularly when we are bringing this bill within the provisions of the summary convictions act, when the Criminal Code provides certain limitations? Having done that, why should we in this particular instance provide for prosecution being taken at any time, not only in the lifetime of the present minister. The minister is not an individual; he is the head of the department.
It is possible that a prosecution could be conducted 20 years after the loan had been made and after it had been repaid. I suggest that is not right. We should not be departing so far from principles which have always guided and governed this country in connection with prosecutions.
This is a quasi-criminal offence. Once we have begun breaking down the precedents that have been established, although, as I have said, probably no injustice would follow from it directly, then some other government of some other party may be in control of Canada and it can say, "Here is a precedent that has been established." The statute of limitations would have been wiped out, and the precedent would have been established by this government; therefore people would say it must be good because it was established by a party which had been in control here, and so on and so forth.

I suggest to the minister again that he give this further consideration and try to amend that clause so as to take out that particularly obnoxious part.

I have no objection to removing the words to which my hon. friend referred a while ago. They occur in the nineteenth and twentieth lines on page 2, beginning after the word "minister":
-or by any person purporting to be acting on his behalf.
In my opinion there is no reason why the minister should not make this certificate, since he would be the one that would have peculiar knowledge of the facts contained in it. If it is the wish of the hon. member who is speaking on behalf of the gentleman who moved the amendment to put that in that form, I should be agreeable to it.

For my colleague, in reply to the minister, there is something in this same paragraph to which I should like to direct the minister's attention. The wording under subclause 1 is:
Any person who makes a statement in an application for a guaranteed farm improvement loan that is false in any material respect . . .
I would gather from that, Mr. Chairman, that there is no question at all of intent here. It is merely a simple statement of fact that is false in any respect. In other words it could be a simple innocent statement in which a person might give some false information on the application. In view of what has been said by my colleague from Digby-Annapolis-Kings it would seem bad enough to have no time limit for the starting of a prosecution even if there were guilty intent, but here there is no time limit under which prosecution can be begun even in the case of an innocent mistake.
I should like to suggest to the minister with respect that in the second line, after it says, "Any person who makes a statement in an application for a guaranteed farm improvement loan",-the words "with intent to defraud" be added. Then it would carry on, "that is false in any material respect."
The addition of those words, "with intent to defraud", would improve the clause very much. As it is at present, a farmer making an innocent mistake in an application could be prosecuted 20 years afterwards and be fined or, if he did not meet the fine, could be sent to jail. I know it is not very likely, but with the wording of the clause at the moment that is what could happen. It does not seem proper that a person should be punished for the quasi-criminal offence of a simple statement of fact and a statement of incrimination. I feel that could easily be cleared up by adding the words "with 67509-327
Farm Improvement Loans Act intent to defraud." As the minister well knows, being in the profession, evidence could be given to prove intent, and I think the clause would be materially improved by making that suggested addition.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR NEW THREE-YEAR POOL, MAXIMUM GUARANTEE OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
It would be difficult to add very much to what the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has said in connection with the shortcomings of this clause. As a matter of fact I welcomed the indication by the Minister of Finance that he feels there is some defect in this clause and is prepared to do something about it. Coming on the heels of what the Prime Minister did last night in dealing with clause 6 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, that gives us some assurance of an indication of a desire to take care of some of these very important small points in connection with legislation of this type.
I for one welcome the indication that these sections are being studied in that manner. I do not think, however, that merely by deleting this one sentence we are going to have the solution of the problem this particular section raises. Although it has been mentioned that a similar section is contained in the Unemployment Insurance Act I cannot help but feel that apparently in the various acts of a similar nature such as the Canadian Farm Loan Act there has been no thought of including such a penalty section.
I have looked at the Canadian Farm Loan Act and I find that, under section 7, (i) and again under section 20, subsection 7, when people use the money improperly the act says that under certain circumstances they must give it back. In coming forward as the minister has to deal with the question of the certificate, he is only doing in that case what I notice is provided for in the Financial Administration Act, chapter 116, section 89, subsection 2, where it says that where money has been improperly used the minister himself gives a certificate to that effect in connection with the improper use of the same. This seems to be going one step further than has been done in similar legislation.
The suggestion made by the hon. member for Oxford was the subject matter for an amendment, as I recall it, previously voted down by the committee. But certainly if this section giving the right to prosecute after several years is going to be retained, I think we might give a second thought to the provision dealing with intent to defraud. Our other penal statutes ordinarily permit us to go back a great length of time if there is proof of intent to defraud. I think the Minister of National Revenue knows that provision is contained in his legislation. There is a place where you stop under one set of

Farm Improvement Loans Act circumstances, but if there is intent to defraud there is permission to continue to go back in order to obtain the evidence and prosecute. So I would say it is a step in the right direction here, the one that has been suggested, but it still does not solve the crucial problem in connection with this legislation.
I might point out one other thing to the Prime Minister. I find that section 6 of this legislation indicates that if this act is passed after March 31 it is to be considered as having come into effect on April 1 of this year. I say we are then making this retroactive legislation.

-in view of the argument I am making. I say this to the Prime Minister as well as to the Minister of Finance, because I recognize what the Prime Minister did last night. Here is an indication that we are making -a particular additional section effective as from April 1; and to anyone having any knowledge of this type of act it is obvious that this is a quasicriminal section. As such it should not be part of a retroactive piece of legislation.
Perhaps in finally arriving at a satisfactory solution to this difficulty, if the legislation is going to include the words dealing with the intent to defraud, and if it is finally going to end up with the deletion of the provision that anyone can certify for the minister, then it may be possible that section 6 as well should be amended in some way to ensure that this particular section is not effective from April 1.
Here is what is happening. It may be that the circumstances upon which a prosecution may later be based may have taken place between April 1 and June 19, when a person has made his application, whatever it is. There may be circumstances which, under
[Mr. Hamilton (York West) .1
this legislation, 20 years from now will result in a prosecution. I say that under those circumstances this very definitely is bringing into effect in a retroactive manner a quasicriminal type of legislation.
I therefore say, Mr. Chairman, that there is a great deal of merit in the amendment that is before the committee at the present time. If that amendment should not be carried, then I commend again to the Minister of Finance the words of the hon. member for Oxford and, prior to that, the amendment which was proposed by the hon. member for Peel. You can still rectify this situation by including the wording "with intent to defraud"; by deleting the words you have suggested should be deleted, and by subsequently amending paragraph 6. Those are things I think any prudent man would take into serious consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR NEW THREE-YEAR POOL, MAXIMUM GUARANTEE OF LOANS, ETC.

Mr. Chairman, there is just a brief word I should like to say. It seems to me that if the minister insists-as I hope he will not-on the retention of subclause 2 in clause 8, the very least he can do-in fact he should not even have to be asked to do it-is to remove the words he has offered to remove from lines nineteen and twenty on page 2. But I do not see how the minister can think that by making that offer he meets the basic objection which has been made from this side of the chamber to subclause 2 of clause 8. After all, the real evil in this clause is in lines thirteen and fourteen where authority is given to commence an action at any time within 12 months from the day on which evidence comes to the knowledge of the minister. All I am suggesting at this moment, Mr. Chairman, is that these things must be looked at separately.
I can hardly conceive that the minister is trying to make a trade, that he is suggesting to the opposition that the amendment moved by the hon. member from Kamloops be dropped in return for the minister's offer to drop these words from lines nineteen and twenty. They are two totally different things. What the minister has offered to drop out is the least objectionable part of this subclause. He has not yet met the argument regarding the most objectionable part of it, namely the authority to enter proceedings for an offence literally at any time provided it is within 12 months after the day on which the evidence comes to the minister's knowledge, no matter when he obtains that evidence. Perhaps we can debate that point under some other heading or in some other relationship, but I believe the two points should be kept separate.

Mr. Chairman, I think the various members who have spoken have made a good case for the passage of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops. When we had this bill before the committee we were told by the deputy minister that the record under this act was exceptionally good in so far as the question of repayment was concerned. Repayments had been good.
In the light of that fact it is hard to understand why the government at this time should see fit to introduce an amendment of this kind. Are they anticipating that conditions are going to be so tough that the farmers in order to get loans are going to be driven to methods that are wrong, and then will that action be hanging over the farmers' heads indefinitely? The farmer will never know whether, 20 years from now, the government may come along and say that he signed the document wrongly, and the minister will then be in a position to take action of any kind within 12 months from that date. It does not seem a very satisfactory condition so far as the farmer is concerned. I cannot understand why the minister should now consider it necessary to introduce this amendment when the act has operated so satisfactorily in the past.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR NEW THREE-YEAR POOL, MAXIMUM GUARANTEE OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not want anyone to misunderstand the reason for this, and there seems to be some misunderstanding. When an application has been granted and a loan made, you must remember that this is a guarantee of the government of Canada. It is not a loan by the government of Canada. There is nothing here comparable to the Canadian farm loan board, in which case the government of Canada makes the loan. In this case the bank makes the loan and all we do is guarantee it under the conditions set down in the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Now, if everything goes well, the money is paid and that is the end of it. We never hear anything more about it.
But when something goes wrong, when default occurs and the bank then asks us to repay the loan or pay the amount of money we guaranteed, that is the first time the government of Canada can have any information about it and can ascertain 67509-327J
19. 1956
Farm Improvement Loans Act whether there has been some kind of misrepresentation such as we describe here. That is the reason it has been thought necessary to ask that the power to prosecute should start from that date and not from the date of the making of the loan by the bank, because we have nothing to do with the original making of the loan.
Under those circumstances I suggest to hon. members that if we are to be responsible for these bank guarantees, surely we ought to be in the position of having the right to prosecute within a very short time, namely 12 months, after the first time the offence comes to our attention.
It would be the reverse if we were dealing directly with the borrower. I quite agree with my hon. friend from York West when he speaks of the Canadian farm loan board. In that case we have the original opportunity to decide whether any fraud has in fact occurred, or any misrepresentation of a material nature. That is the reason for this. There is no suggestion, and I am sorry to say this, that there has not been difficulty in the past. There have been many cases in which we have found that there has been an effort made to conceal the true facts from the bank in the first instance. I do not know why anyone considers that the government of Canada should not be in the position of having some power to act, both in the punitive sense as well as in the sense of, shall I say, avoiding trouble, in the provisions of a statute of this kind.
If I may answer some of the questions already put, no one supposes that if an applicant described a farm lot number incorrectly, any magistrate would, in any sense of the word, convict. But the point is that if there is a deliberate misrepresentation of assets or if there is a deliberate statement that the money will be spent for the payment of certain liabilities and later it is found the money has been diverted for other purposes, it seems to us there ought to be a penalty for that because this is a beneficial statute in favour of farmers, just as there are beneficial statutes in favour of other people. There ought to be a proper method of showing that the taxpayers' money is not to be used lightly in this way.

speechtext: In view of what the minister has just said, unless I have misunderstood him he has clearly indicated that the whole intent of this section is to deal with intent to defraud and not with an innocent mistake. The way the section is worded, however, it appears clear that any farmer who makes some mistake, albeit an innocent one, in his application could be prosecuted some time afterward. In view of what the minister has

Farm Improvement Loans Act said I think it should be made clear that the section is aimed at the intent to defraud, and I cannot see anything objectionable in making that request.
Mr. Pallet!: I think the Minister of Finance has made a very good case for taking the section right out altogether. He has said that the government guarantees the loan to the bank. Then what do the banks do for the government? Do they not accept any responsibility themselves when making these loans? They are the people who interview the applicants and they should be the people who have the responsibility for certifying to the government that these loans are proper loans. The government is trying to go right through the person who is receiving the profit from the loan to the farmer who is obliged to borrow the money in the first instance. When you suggest that you cannot find out what is wrong with the application until default has occurred, that indicates to me that the people whom you have authorized to make these loans are not properly carrying out their duties.
If that has been the history, then I suggest there should be some penal provision against the people making the profit and not the people who seek to get the loans. Obviously the breakdown is in the people who are receiving the applications not taking the care before the loans are made that they would take with a loan that was not guaranteed. Of course it is possible that the recent position in which the minister has been placed has caused him to think like a banker rather than like a member of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Never.

As has already been so well said, you would not permit a penalty provision of this type in the Criminal Code which was reviewed in this house and by a committee of people who are handling the affairs of justice in this country. At the same time you say here is one small section of the community that you are going to discriminate against. You say you have already discriminated against another section, but that does not excuse this action. Are we not going to look to the people in whom we have placed confidence to carry out their duties?
I say seriously to the minister that you are allowing something to continue, as has already been said, that is strange and foreign to our method of administering the law. You are making retroactive legislation with a penalty provision. You are putting a provision in this act that you would not permit in the Criminal Code and you are not taking any concrete steps to say to the banks, "If you make bad loans we will not guarantee them; before we will guarantee your loans


you have to certify that these loans are made on a proper basis". The applicant's responsibility is to the banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I just clear the question of retroactivity. I think every hon. member who has read clause 6 will realize the purpose of the retroactive provision. The Farm Improvement Loans Act ran out on March 31. This bill was introduced before that date for the purpose of continuing the benefit of these loans to the farm community. I have no doubt there have been loans made since that date, and the purpose of the legislation is to validate the guarantees that would be made for those particular loans.

Mr. Chairman, the minister now suggests it is because of the guarantee angle of this loan that he wants the penalty clause. I suggest to him that the fisherman's loan is a guaranteed loan but there is no penalty clause in that act at all. Although I realize the Canadian Farm Loan Act is not a guaranteed loan act there is no penalty clause in that act either. The minister is saying that this legislation is similar to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Is he suggesting that it is comparable with the Unemployment Insurance Act?
The minister appears to think he is giving the farmers something under this act. He is not giving them anything; he is only guaranteeing the loan at the bank. Out of loans amounting to $582 million the loss to date has been $285,000. Is the minister suggesting that all the farmers who take those loans are to be subjected to this clause just because $285,000 has been lost out of $582 million? Must all the farmers who take loans under this act have this on their shoulders for the rest of their lives? I ask that question advisedly, because it could be for the rest of their lives. They could have this hanging over their heads, with the fear that they could be brought into court.
As the hon. member for Oxford said, it might be purely a mistake, yet under this clause it could be proven that it was a false statement, and whether it was a mistake or intentional they could be subject to a fine of $500 or imprisonment if they could not pay. It is ridiculous. Not only is it ridiculous, it is the most terrible thing I have seen in this house for some time. Especially is that true when there is no penalty at all in the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act or the Canadian Farm Loan Act.
The minister is suggesting that this is similar to the Unemployment Insurance Act, which I suggest is an insurance act and not a loan act. It is something given to people. They pay their premiums, naturally, but it

is something given to them in lieu of employment. It is not comparable at all.
It is not a gift; it is insurance.
The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate would do well to sit quietly in his seat for just a few moments.
I take up less time in the house than the hon. gentleman does.
Sitting in the house is not everything. Sometimes we like to see people sit quietly, too.
So do we.

I suggest this legislation is different from the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is something that is unknown in this house; it is foreign legislation to this house. I am not a lawyer but I have heard it discussed enough to know-and I think all members will agree with me-that it is a foreign type of legislation. The minister has not given us enough justification to allow it to go through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I just answer my hon. friend briefly. There is a penalty clause in the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act, though it is not the same as this. My hon. friend should be aware of the fact that there are penalty clauses in all the borrowing and guaranteeing statutes that we have, so far as I know.
I do not think I agree with him that we are not giving the farmer anything. I think the farming community are appreciative of the benefits of the guarantee at the bank under these circumstances; at least a great many of them have used it. It is quite true that we have not had to pay very much in the way of losses; and that only establishes the fact that it is unlikely that the farming community have had too much trouble in making their payments, and they will go on using the advantages of borrowing under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I certainly think this is of advantage to the farmer. We are increasing the amount of the loan he can have from the bank. I am a little surprised that the hon. member would say that we are not doing anything for the farmer.

I did not say we are doing nothing for the farmer; I said you are not giving anything to the farmer, and you are not giving him a thing. He is borrowing money under a guaranteed loan. He has paid it all back with the exception of $285,000, and you suggest you are giving him something. You are giving him a service, that is all.

I wish I could get some sort of answer out of the minister which would clear up some misunderstanding that seems to be in the minds of hon. members. Is it the intention of the minister under this section to punish applicants for an innocent mistake, or is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Of course not.
Why does it say so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It does not say so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?

The minister has just told us that it is not the intention of the government to punish people for innocent misrepresentation. I am glad to hear that statement. The minister is a lawyer and well knows that the courts must take the specific wording of the act. The section says:
Any person who makes a statement in an application for a guaranteed farm improvement loan that is false in any material respect . . .
And so on. It does not say "false statement of intent"; it says "is false in any material respect". It refers to something that is false regardless of the intent behind it. The remarks the minister has just made certainly have little relationship or little relevancy to what it says in the section. I am afraid I cannot understand it. The minister also said a few moments ago that the farmers would probably take advantage of the act. No doubt they will. If they were familiar with the language of this legislation I doubt whether they would be so anxious to take advantage of the provisions of this act, because some of these amendments put the guarantor of those loans in almost a worse position than the well-known character in "The Merchant of Venice".
Mr. Pallet!: Will the minister indicate whether he would be willing to insert the words "with intent to defraud"? As you know, no court can go behind the act and read Hansard to find out what the members of the committee meant when the words were inserted in the legislation.
In reply to questions this afternoon the minister has said that it is not the intention, where there is innocent misrepresentation, to charge anybody under this section. I suggest that for clarification the words "with intent to defraud" should be inserted. Nothing would be lost by inserting those words. It is a very simple thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have already disposed of that in the committee on a former occasion, Mr. Chairman. But, in any event, may I point out to my hon. friend that the wording is

Farm Improvement Loans Act pretty clear. It says, "false in any material respect". No magistrate nor any county court judge dealing with this section is going to fine a person who made an innocent mistake about a particular matter that is not material, guilty under the act.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance by this very act takes the magistrate's discretion completely away from him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No.
Mr. Pallet!: Yes, he does. That is the effect of the wording of this legislation. The hon. member for York Centre has just inserted a comment. I am quite prepared to sit down and listen to what he has to say.

As a matter of fact, any county court judge will determine what is material. Absolute authority is vested in him to say whether it is true or false. The county court judge may determine whether or not it is a material fact. Consequently I think the hon. member's argument is quite redundant.

If the hon. member reads the legislation he will find that the case first comes before a magistrate, who is not a county court judge. I think it is generally accepted that the people who are appointed to these positions are not all legally trained. If you mean to say that the innocent misrepresentation is not to be charged it is of no consequence to add the four words, "with intent to defraud". It seems to me if that is what you mean but you are not prepared to put it in writing, it is not what you mean by the words you have just used.

On more than one occasion I have heard magistrates say, "I have all sympathy but the act says so and so". They go entirely by the act. I do not see why the minister should be antagonistic and refuse to add these words, "with intent to defraud". They will take nothing from the bill; they will add to it. They will protect the individual. Some person may get a loan processed and, through no fault of his, make a mistake. The magistrate can say, "I must go by the act". I believe there is much merit in the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Kamloops, and its acceptance would go a long way toward alleviating the present difficulties.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the committee ready for the question on the amendment?
Mr. Pallet!: No. I think we should deal with this at greater length. There have been charges that the opposition obstructs, and it is events like this which cause us to obstruct. It is our intention to do so in situations such as this. I for one intend to speak as many times as I possibly can until ten

o'clock tonight in an effort to make this act one that will protect the people of this country and not oppress them. This is a clause that is oppressing a certain segment of the population of this country. The minister does not know what is in a magistrate's mind, nor does he know what is in the mind of the minister sitting next to him or of anyone working for him. As one hon. member suggests, perhaps the minister does not even know what is in his own mind; I do not know.
I think what we propose is a very simple matter. The bill certainly would pass this house very readily if it were inserted. I think the complete deletion of this part of the section would be preferable to anything that has been proposed, but failing that I would simply point out it seems to me the minister has established a little mental block over there. Perhaps he feels he is going to lose face or something. The government has lost a great deal of face in the past few weeks and a little more is not going to hurt it that much. Personally, however, I do not think it would lose face, in fact it would gain a bit, if it were to accede to a proper request.

Mr. Chairman, I always try to be reasonable, and if I make a mistake or get the wrong interpretation I am always willing to change my mind. I have listened carefully to the minister this afternoon and the remarks he has made on the clause. He made a statement a few minutes ago which I believe was supported by the hon. member for York Centre, that it was up to the magistrate, the judge or the officer trying the matter, to determine whether or not a thing was material.
I have had a reasonable amount of experience in practising law before magistrates and in county courts, and I would like to point out to the minister there are two blades to the scissors, so to speak, which the magistrate would have to consider with respect to the statement made in the application. The first one is whether in fact the statement that was made was material. In other words, did it or did it not affect the granting of the loan in the first place; and second, was it false? The magistrate or the officer trying the case might very well decide it was material and the next question that would arise would be whether or not the statement was false. There is no information in this section, and the minister certainly offers us no explanation regarding that. There is no intimation that the falseness of the statement must contain an element of intent in order to be punishable. The way it is set out here the falseness of a statement, even if it is made in innocence, is subject to punishment.

As the minister well knows, this comes under the summary convictions act, and if the fine cannot be paid the person is sent to jail. As far as I can see the minister has certainly offered us no explanation.

I do not think the minister need worry about losing face, because last night we had a shining example of what can be accomplished by an argument being put forth and received in a reasonable manner.
I have had a little argument on the side here with one hon. member who suggests this amendment is protecting the one dishonest man in a hundred, but there is nothing remarkable about that in connection with what is known as British justice. It has been said over and over again that it is better that a hundred guilty people should go free than to convict one innocent person.
It may seem a little remarkable that this large house is spending half an hour on this particular point, but this is certainly the place where we can get down to fundamentals so far as our laws are concerned. I do not think anyone is going to object to this type of legislation or to the fact that there may be 20 years in which to prosecute if the words "with intent to defraud" are included.
I hope the minister will seriously consider what is put forward here in the form of an amendment as an alternative to the present wording, along with the deletion of the words he has suggested further down in the section. Let us not worry about losing face. As a matter of fact, I think it will make the government look a great deal more substantial if it agrees to suggestions which are worth while.

Before the question is put I would like to place one point before the minister. We have disposed of the amendment striking out all of clause 2, which is an amendment I think the government should have accepted. I return again to the thesis I proposed a few moments ago, to the effect that it is absolutely wrong to have a criminal act with no limitation in it whatever. The committee has decided we cannot accept the striking out of clause 2. The minister has also pointed out, and I can follow this, that
19/ 1956
Farm Improvement Loans Act it may be some considerable time after the loan is made before it comes to the attention of the minister that there has been misrepresentation or fraud.
There is nothing in the section which says that. The section is an open end transaction in so far as prosecution is concerned. As I say again, I am not suggesting that this would be done but I do think it is so contrary to the principles of law that we should not permit something which may or may not be twisted by individuals.
The minister knows by looking at the clause that it would be possible for a prosecution to be started long after the maturity of the loan, long after the loan had been paid. There is nothing to tie it in with the loan. The minister said a moment ago that perhaps this would not come to his attention until the loan had been paid off. I cannot conceive that it would, because ordinarily these loans are payable by instalments.
I do not intend to move a formal amendment now because I realize that if it does not commend itself to the minister it will not be accepted by the committee, but we do feel strongly about this thing. I do not propose this simply for the purpose of delaying matters, but may I read the section:
(3) Proceedings for an offence under this section may be commenced at any time within twelve months from the day on which evidence-
That again leaves it wide open as to what may or may not be evidence or what may or may not be information. They are two different things, as the minister well knows. When the minister has decided that he has evidence that might be, shall we say, six months, a year or two years from the time he first got a letter from the bank manager saying there was a little trouble over this thing. Let me read the clause again:
Proceedings for an offence under this section may be commenced at any time within twelve months from the day on which evidence, sufficient in the opinion of the minister to justify prosecution for the offence, comes to his knowledge.
I suggest to the minister that at least we close that in, that we do not have it wide open. I would suggest that he put a proviso at the end providing that such prosecution shall be instituted within twelve months from the due date or maturity date of the said loan. In other words the prosecution would have to be commenced within a definite period.
I understand that there are two classes of loans. Where a loan is made for the purchase of land it might run for as long as 10 years. If you accept the principle of a limitation period, then I would agree that that would be an improvement and we would not be perpetuating a completely wrong principle.

Farm Improvement Loans Act In view of everything the minister has said, surely if there were a limitation period of twelve months from the maturity date of the loan or from when the loan was due, and if he had no evidence of wrongdoing before that time, then certainly he should not be able to prosecute afterwards because the evidence would be so flimsy that it would not warrant prosecution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think perhaps my hon. friend is labouring under a minor misapprehension. We never hear about these loans when they are paid. It is when they are not paid that we hear about them. We are not concerned with the farmer who pays off his loan, and I do not suppose the bank is either. At any rate they never come within our ken. It is only when we are called upon to pay the guarantee that we become interested.

Would not twelve months
from the maturity date take care of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have been waiting for a long time to move an amendment which fits in with the act here. This would add a further subclause 5 which would read:
(5) Proceedings in respect of an offence under this section may not be instituted later than three years from the time when the subject matter of the proceedings arose.
There would then be two limitations; there is the limitation in subclause 3 that proceedings must be taken within twelve months, and then in any event there would be a limitation of three years beyond which prosecution could not be taken.
If the minister had said that earlier instead of sitting on it like a hen on an egg it might have been better.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am afraid that my obedience to the rules of the house make it impossible for me to move an amendment until we reach the point at which it can be moved.

The minister has stated that the government knows nothing about these loans unless they are not paid. I do not think that is quite true. Surely the department would have some idea of the number of applications. Are not copies sent to the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Of course we get notice of the amount of money involved in our guarantees from month to month, but we have no knowledge of a particular loan.
Have you not a copy of the application form that goes in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are kept in the bank, and we are only notified of the person who has the guaranteed loan.
Just the name of the person?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The name, the address and the amount.
You do not have a copy of the application for loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The application is not made to the government, it is made to the bank. Apparently my hon. friend forgets the origin of the legislation.
The minister is not sitting on another egg in connection with offences of fraud?
Do I understand that the minister proposes to introduce an amendment deleting the words "or by any person purporting to be acting in his behalf"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I said that I would do that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Have I that amendment in writing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sorry; I will write it out.

In view of the two amendments that are to be made, any remarks that I made about the effect of clause 6, which is to follow, being retroactive and being detrimental could be withdrawn. There would be no necessity for dealing with it.

I move:
That clause 5 be amended by striking out of lines 19 and 20 the words "or by any person purporting to be acting on his behalf".

I wonder if there would be any confusion in connection with line 24, which reads:
-without proof of the signature or of the official character of the person appearing to have signed the document-
Would that still be in order now that it deals only with the minister himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Amendment agreed to.

I move:
That clause 5 be further amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
" (5) Proceedings in respect of an offence under this section may not be instituted later than three years from the time when the subject matter of the proceedings arose."

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am certainly not going to quarrel over one year in view of the fact that the minister has agreed to a principle that has been argued from this side of the house. But I should like to point out that before he got to his feet with this amendment I was going to ask him to take a look at Bill No. 82, which we passed earlier this session, having to do with guaranteed bank loans to farmers with respect to grain stored on farms. The reason I was going to ask him to

look at that was to draw his attention to the section having to do with offences and penalties, which is section 9. If he is looking at the bill he will find that it had three subsections when it was presented, but he will recall that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had a colleague move the deletion of subsection 3. However, the relevant subsection, subsection 2, reads:
A prosecution under subsection (1) may be instituted at any time within two years from the time when the subject matter of the complaint arose.
It was my purpose to suggest that that language was a little better than the language about information coming to the knowledge of the minister. The minister seems to have picked it up here, but why has he put in three years instead of two? If two years were sufficient in the case of the guaranteed bank loan on grain stored on farms, why would not two years be sufficient in this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Even my hon. friend can find the answer, if he just goes on for two more sentences in what he is reading, and that is that he is dealing with a nine months' loan in the one case and in the other with perhaps a ten-year loan.

Since' the minister has been reasonable in dealing with this matter and has offered an amendment which at least recognizes the principle we were urging, I wonder whether he would not on his own accord consider the matter urged by the hon. member for Peel a few moments ago about the intent to defraud. I realize that technically it was voted on the other night and therefore the discussion of it might be out of order, but there is even more than the hon. member for Peel pointed out. If the person makes a statement that is false in any material respect, that is bad enough. It may or may not be a mistake. But it says:
... or who uses the proceeds of such loan for a purpose other than that stated in his application . . .
It is all very well to say that a magistrate would use common sense; he probably would. But I can imagine a man getting a loan for a tractor, shall we say, coming into town, paying for the tractor, perhaps having $5.05 left over and making a purchase with that $5.05 to take home. I am sure he would not set that forth in his application. Of course if he were a prohibitionist he might use the $5.05 to buy his wife a birthday present that certainly would not be set forth in the application, yet he would be technically guilty of an offence.
The minister says there is no intention of prosecuting a man unless he has deliberately 67509-328
Farm Improvement Loans Act defrauded. We know very well that this minister would not authorize that, but why have it wide open that way if that is the intention? Why should we not insert "with intent to defraud"? Then we would have maintained a principle of law which, although it has been remedied to a substantial extent this afternoon, yet I think is wide open in that one particular sense. I should hope the minister would give consideration to inserting those words, and then I think the bill would be satisfactory in every respect.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On the same point, may I again ask the minister to look at the wording of clause 9 of Bill No. 82, the very first part of which reads:
Every person who, after the coming into force of this act, in respect of a guaranteed loan
(a) knowingly makes any misrepresentation in any application . . .
It seems to me that if the government earlier this session brought in a bill having to do with guaranteed bank loans and put in the word "knowingly", it might consider putting the same word or words having the same meaning in this comparable piece of legislation.

I wonder whether the minister really read this bill before it was put before us. I refer to a statement made on May 1, as recorded on page 3467 of Hansard, in which he said:
I was not a member of the banking and commerce committee, as I believe my friend was, but my recollection is that there have been no convictions although I would not be sure as to that.
If the minister recalls, this bill did not go before the banking and commerce committee; it was referred to the committee on agriculture. The statement by the minister at that time perhaps indicated that he was not following the course of this bill or the preparation of it as closely as he might have been. With that in mind, giving him the benefit of the doubt that perhaps this particular aspect of this clause did not occur to him, there is nothing wrong with that, if that is the situation. We appreciate that with his vast duties he perhaps cannot examine every detail, and sometimes things might escape his attention; but, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre have pointed out, other acts have "knowingly" in them, and it seems such a small point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for his generosity. All money bills that are referred to committees go to the banking and commerce committee. I said in the house that this would go to the banking and commerce

Farm Improvement Loans Act committee but, on the urging of hon. members opposite, I changed that to agriculture and forgot temporarily that I had done so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the clause as amended carry?
Mr. Pallet!: I think we have to explore the other aspects of this a little further. Is there any particular reason the government advances at this time why one section of the community, the agricultural section, should be set apart and why we should say that we are applying the principles of the Criminal Code and various acts against all sections of the community but we are applying them differently against farmers, that we are required to prove certain things against other persons but a farmer is automatically guilty until he proves himself innocent?
Under this bill you say we are going to let the banks lend more money, that loans up to $5,000 will be guaranteed, but we shall be taking away a right from the farmers. It does not matter how much money is given them; rights are more important than money in the building of any society. You cannot buy a right. You have no proper authority to take a right away from them. This is a small but important group of the community, and it is entitled to the protection to which any other groups of the community are entitled.
It may be said that there are two other acts which contain the provision, and it is hoped to put it in a third one. That argument falls because you are repeating a wrong, which is never a correct thing to do. It seems that we would lose nothing and gain much by recognizing that here is a principle which should apply to the agricultural group in this country as well as to any other.

There has been a good deal of discussion on this matter this afternoon. My hon. friend from Peel has just mentioned that in this case the burden of proof has been shifted. Actually there is no burden of proof here at all. It is a simple statement of fact. The burden of proof has been shifted to the accused. Even if a provision were put in that, if he could present evidence that he was not making the statement with any intent to defraud, he could be exonerated, that would be something; but it does not even go that far. It just says "if the statement is in fact false." It is like the provisions of some provincial statutes I can think of that give no discretion to the court.
There are only two things that have to be shown; that the statement is (a) material and (b) false. There is nothing about intent.


If it is merely a false statement, regardless of intention, the person must be punished and can be sent to jail. The minister has already told us on several occasions that it is not the intention of the government to do that, but that is what the bill says.
I suppose there is no use labouring the point. The minister has evidently made up his mind that he is not going to do anything about the wording. I cannot understand why he would take that attitude.

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Indian Act to provide for a number of changes in connection with the administration of the act; and to provide further that the Minister of Finance may from time to time advance to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration out of 67509-328J
Indian Act

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman could not resist the temptation to point that out.
The purpose of this resolution is to authorize the introduction of a bill that has only one section which has any financial implications. In what I say today I am going to deal solely with the section that has financial implications because it seems to me it would be simply a waste of the time of the committee and of the house to deal with a hypothetical bill before anyone has the right to look at it.
The revolving fund that is referred to in this resolution is a fund which, under the act, amounted to $350,000. Last year, when the estimates of my department were before the committee of supply, I asked to have this amount increased to $650,000. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will remember this proceeding because he took some exception not to the substance but to the form of what was done at that time. I point that out because, from the resolution, it appears that the amount of the fund is being increased to $1 million from $350,000 whereas, in fact, it is being increased from $650,000 to $1 million. But the $650,000 is not in the Indian Act; it is in the appropriation act of last year.
These loans which are made out of this revolving fund are advanced to Indians to assist them in establishing themselves in agriculture, forestry, fishing, in setting up business in handicrafts, for getting equipment and facilities for guiding, trapping and a good many other miscellaneous pursuits. The purpose of the loans is to make it possible for Indians-who, because of the protection

Indian Act
they are given under the Indian Act, are also under a disability about borrowing in the ordinary way-to get money on reasonable terms in order to supplement their traditional mode of livelihood.
I would remind the committee that the Indian population of this country, without any addition by immigration and indeed with a steady diminution because of enfranchisement, is growing faster than the rest of the population, whereas their additional means of livelihood are actually being diminished as settlement moves farther north or because of defence installations in some cases or for other reasons. In view of this development, I think one of the most important internal problems we have in this country, and certainly morally there is no more important internal problem for the rest of us, is to do our utmost in every practical way we can to see that the Indians have every opportunity we can give them of developing new ways of supporting themselves and living in a self-respecting manner as ordinary members of the community.
I do think this revolving fund has done a great deal to make it possible for the more enterprising Indians, those with a bit more initiative, to do that. I have a great deal of material here about the number of loans, the record of repayment and other material of that sort. The record of repayment is remarkably good and the number of bad loans is very small. I do not really think it would serve any particularly useful purpose for me to attempt to put it all on the record, but I would be glad to answer any questions any member of the committee may wish to ask.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
So far as the latter part of the resolution is concerned, the only part with which the minister dealt, I think all of us are very pleased to see that there is to be an increase from the present statutory provision of $350,000 to $1 million for this revolving fund, out of which loans can be made to bands or to individual Indians. I fully agree with what the minister said, that much more needs to be done along this line than has been done in the past so far as enabling Indians to better themselves is concerned. The provisions of section 69, under which this money is lent, read as follows:
(a)	to make loans to bands, groups of Indians or individual Indians for the purchase of farm implements, machinery, livestock, motor vehicles, fishing equipment, seed grain, fencing materials, materials to be used in native handicrafts, any other equipment, and gasoline and other petroleum products, or for the making of repairs or the payment of wages, or
(b)	to expend or to lend money for the carrying out of co-operative projects on behalf of Indians.
The minister said he would be glad to answer questions, and I think it would be of
[Mr. Pickersgill.j
some interest to the committee if, before we have finished with the resolution, he could let us know how many loans had been made under this act. How many are in effect at the present time or the latest period for which he has figures? In other words, to what extent has use been made of this fund of $350,000? I should also be very interested in knowing the maximum amounts which have been made available to any particular Indian. As a matter of fact, I think one of the weaknesses in this provision of the Indian Act is that the amount which any particular Indian and even band of Indians could get, particularly for the purchase of livestock or farm implements in the west was too small.
I do not know much about the situation so far as the east is concerned. I know that a considerable number of Indians on the reserves with which I am familiar have been definitely handicapped in making any economic or material progress as a result of the fact that they were unable to secure a sufficient number of farm implements or a sufficient amount of livestock to what I might call set up economic farming on the portion of the reserve which was allotted to them. In other words, I do not think there is any doubt that up to date not nearly enough has been done along the lines which this particular section of the act envisages.
The Indians have not been assisted nearly to the extent they might have been or, in many cases, to the extent they wanted to be. So far as my information goes, this probably has not been the result, at least up until recently, of the fact that there was not a sufficient amount of money in the revolving fund. The difficulty has been that the regulations under which these loans have been made were too stringent, or the total amount which could or would be given to a particular Indian was too small. I would hope that the regulations as well as the legislation itself would be changed and that an increase would be made in the amount of loan which would be available to an Indian.
I think that is particularly necessary in view of the fact we have had a constant process of inflation going on in this country. This has been recognized in the amendments to the farm loan act which we have had this session and in the amendments to the various other acts such as the Veterans' Land Act, which have been before the house recently. In all these cases the total amount of the loan has been increased in recognition of the fact that inflation has taken place. Whereas even seven or eight years ago a loan of $5,000 may have been sufficient for the

purpose of the legislation, at the present time it is not sufficient. I believe the same principle should be applied to the Indian Act and the regulations amended accordingly, so that a greater amount will be available.
In addition to that I would hope that the fact that the total amount available is being increased to $1 million means that the department itself has decided on a much more vigorous policy so far as making use of this provision is concerned, and will give perhaps a more vigorous leadership than has been the case in the past in encouraging Indians to make use of this provision and get into various activities in which they can make a living for themselves.
In so far as the first part of the resolution is concerned, it reads merely:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Indian Act to provide for a number of changes in connection with the administration of the act-
One would think from this wording that probably the changes are not of very much importance. In introducing this resolution the minister did not say anything about those changes. In fact I think he said they would not be of much interest to the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
The statement in the resolution concerning certain administrative changes is a very poor description of what is involved in these various changes. My information may not be correct, but I understand that copies of the proposed changes were shown to a meeting of Indians which was held in Ottawa last winter. I was very glad to hear that this meeting had been held, and that the proposed changes had been shown to the Indians. I think it is essential, in dealing with our Indians, that their cooperation be secured, and that when changes in the act are contemplated they should be
Indian Act
consulted and their advice should be taken in regard to any changes which may be proposed.
However, what I understand or what I have heard as a result of these delegates coming back and circulating their experiences among their comrades and others, is that the general purpose of many of the changes proposed is to shift authority and power to make decisions from the governor in council, where it resides under the Indian Act as it is at the present time, to the minister himself. As far as I can gather, the Indians look on such a change with very considerable trepidation. They consider their interests would be much better protected if the power of decision in regard to these matters were to remain with the governor in council rather than be shifted into the hands of one man, the minister. These changes, if they are as I understand them, represent an increase in the arbitrary power of the minister and his agents-
